personality_one_liner: A cinematic, premium pre-production suite using deep charcoal and muted gold to feel like a high-end film set tool.

spacing.rule: Generous spacing for headers and sections to create a cinematic feel. Tighter, precise grouping inside technical shot list cards.

do's: Use heavy glass with a dark translucent tint (>=75% opacity) over background images for hero headers.
Apply frosted glass to the bottom sticky CTA containers in wizard steps.
Apply frosted glass to the bottom tab bar.
Use glass headers when scrolling through long shot lists.
dont's: Never use glass for dense data rows or form inputs.
Don't stack glass on top of glass.
Do not use glass if the background is a solid color; use surfaceSecondary instead.

screens.name: Dashboard
screens.purpose: A premium cinematic overview of recent projects and production stats.

states.empty: Glassy card with 'clapperboard' image, prompting the user to create their first production.
states.error: Muted error text with a 'Reload' button.

screens.layout: Hero section at the top featuring a blurred cinematic camera lens background overlaid with a heavy dark glass greeting and high-level stats. Below, a horizontal scrolling list of recent projects using image-first cards. A 'Templates' gallery section below.

screens.name: New Project Wizard
screens.purpose: Step-by-step setup for a new production (Info, Settings, Creative, Generate).

states.error: Inline error messaging below failed inputs.

screens.layout: Immersive full-screen wizard. A top glass header indicating step progress (e.g., 'Step 1 of 4'). Form fields are clean, large, and minimal on surfaceTertiary backgrounds. A prominent sticky primary CTA pinned at the bottom in a frosted glass container over the scrolling form content.

screens.name: Project Editor (Storyboard & Shot List)
screens.purpose: The core workspace for filmmakers to view the visual storyboard and technical shot list.

states.loading: Skeleton rows indicating shot list loading.
states.empty: Graphic of empty storyboard sketches with a 'Generate AI Storyboard' CTA.
states.error: Error state with a retry icon and text.

screens.layout: Top navigation header with a segmented control to toggle between 'Storyboard' (Grid) and 'Shot List' (List). Storyboard view uses a 2-col or 1-col image-first card grid (large aspect-ratio thumbnails). Shot List view uses a dense vertical card list. Each row shows a small thumbnail left, Shot ID and description right. Collapsible card design to reveal framing, lens, and audio details without cluttering the main list. Drag handles visible for reordering.

dashboard_hero_bg.alt: Cinematic camera lens with dramatic dark lighting

empty_projects_clapperboard.alt: Black and white film clapperboard on dark background

instructions_to_main_agent: Strictly follow the color palette. This is a premium cinematic app. BANNED: all blues, indigos, purples, and navies. Use the defined charcoal/slate neutral base with the muted cinematic gold (Antique Gold) accent.

Implement the '6 Glass / Luxe DARK' personality. Use Cormorant Garamond for large, dramatic elegant headers and wizard titles to feel like a high-end film tool. Use Geist for all UI text, labels, and the dense shot list for maximum readability.
For the Project Editor, build a segmented control in the header to toggle between 'Storyboard' (image-first cards) and 'Shot List' (dense list rows).

In the Shot List table view, ensure rows are card-based vertical lists with thumbnail, shot ID, description, and status visible at a glance. Make rows collapsible to reveal deeper metadata (lens, angle, movement, audio) without cluttering the view.

In the New Project wizard, ensure the 'Continue' CTA is housed in a sticky frosted glass container at the bottom of the screen, floating above the scrolling form fields so users don't have to scroll to the end to proceed.
Background images MUST have a vertical gradient scrim (transparent to >=75% surface/surfaceInverse) applied before rendering text on top to ensure WCAG readability.
Only use weight 400 or 500 for fonts. Do not use bold/heavy cuts, even for the serif display font. Hierarchy is achieved through size, not weight.
